text: Curcumin's mild blood-thinning effect could theoretically add to apixaban's, though this pairing is less studied than curcumin with warfarin.

text: Vitamin K works against warfarin directly — it's the same pathway warfarin blocks — so a vitamin K2 supplement can make warfarin noticeably less effective at thinning your blood. This is one of the best-documented supplement-drug interactions there is.
src: Extensive clinical literature; warfarin prescribing information

Long-term metformin use can lower vitamin B12 levels over time — this is common enough that many people on metformin have their B12 checked periodically. Supplementing isn't dangerous; it's often specifically recommended.
Chromium supplements may add to metformin's blood-sugar-lowering effect, which could raise the chance of blood sugar dropping too low, especially at higher supplement doses.

text: Acid-reducing medication like omeprazole can reduce how much calcium your body absorbs, especially from calcium carbonate — citrate forms like this one are absorbed somewhat better without needing stomach acid.
Long-term use of acid-reducing medication like omeprazole can lower B12 absorption, since stomach acid helps release B12 from food and some supplement forms.

The FDA has warned that long-term use (typically over a year) of acid-reducing medication like omeprazole can cause low magnesium levels, which can become serious. This is the medication depleting magnesium, not a direct interaction with the supplement itself.
Stomach acid helps your body absorb iron. Long-term use of acid-reducing medication like omeprazole can reduce how much iron gets absorbed.
Thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide reduce how much calcium your body eliminates in urine. Combined with a calcium supplement, this can occasionally push blood calcium higher than normal.

Vitamin D increases calcium absorption, and thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide already reduce how much calcium you lose in urine — combined, this can occasionally push blood calcium too high.

ARBs like losartan can raise potassium levels in your blood on their own. Adding a potassium supplement on top can push levels too high — worth checking with a doctor, especially at higher supplement doses.

Furosemide causes your body to lose potassium, which is why potassium supplements are sometimes specifically recommended alongside it. Not dangerous on its own — just worth matching the amount to what your doctor advises.

Furosemide can lower magnesium levels along with potassium, which is why a magnesium supplement is sometimes recommended alongside it. Not dangerous — just worth coordinating with your doctor's guidance.

Long-term steroid use like prednisone increases the risk of bone thinning and reduces how well your body absorbs calcium — this is why calcium is often specifically recommended for people on long-term steroids.
